Whether this process produces accurate beliefs or merely consensus depends on how people combine private evidence with their neighbors' judgments. Two families of computational models make distinct assumptions: DeGroot models synchronously average available opinions, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) models update beliefs sequentially from neighbor-specific prediction errors. These accounts have not been directly compared in controlled social networks with repeated real-time interaction. We compared them using trial-by-trial choices from two previously published experiments involving 209 and 760 participants, respectively. Participants repeatedly revised predictions in networks differing in size and topology. We fitted unweighted and degree-weighted variants of both model families and compared them using random-effects Bayesian model selection. We then used simulations parameterized by the fitted models to assess network-level accuracy and consensus. In both datasets, a DeGroot variant had the strongest group-level model evidence, although the best-fitting rule varied across individuals. Network topology also mattered: unweighted DeGroot best explained behavior in most structures, whereas degree-weighted DeGroot was favored in the highly centralized Royal Family network. Simulations showed that DeGroot averaging generally generated more consensus than naïve sequential RL, while degree-weighted RL could achieve similar accuracy and consensus depending on the assumed information-sampling order. Topology further shaped collective outcomes: hub-dominated networks could reach high consensus despite relatively low accuracy.
